papers.title: The Digital-Energy Recomposition of the Kitchin Cycle: Exploratory Evidence from U.S. IT and Irish Data-Centre Series (1995-2025)
papers.abstract: Using quarterly FRED and CSO Ireland data over 1995Q1-2025Q4, we examine whether U.S.\ IT investment and Irish data-centre electricity are recomposing the Kitchin cycle around energy- and compute-backed assets. Three findings stand out. First, a Quandt-Andrews sup-Wald test locates a significant break in the U.S.\ IT-GDP correlation at 2014Q3 (sup-W $= 9.69$; $r$ falls from $+0.45$ to $-0.12$); the Fisher $r$-to-$z$ test survives Bonferroni adjustment ($z = +3.11$, $p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.006$), whereas the analogous test on the imposed Cloud-vs-AI boundary does not ($p_{\text{Bonf}} = 0.164$), so ``Strategic Decoupling'' pre-dates the AI Era by approximately six years. Second, in Ireland the synchronous AI-Era correlation between metered data-centre electricity and Real GDP is large ($r = +0.41$, $N = 16$) but \emph{collapses to $r \approx 0$ when Real GDP is replaced by Real GNP}, suggesting the headline is largely an artefact of the shared multinational tax-structure footprint between hyperscaler operations and Irish gross output. Third, the Irish cross-correlation profile is asymmetric in the opposite direction to a leading-indicator reading: the largest positive coefficients cluster on the $k < 0$ side (GDP precedes data-centre load), so compute capacity is better read as coincident or moderately lagging. Given the small AI-Era samples and the absence of a quarterly multinational-adjusted aggregate such as GNI*, all coefficients are exploratory; subject to these caveats, the U.S.\ Kitchin cycle is best dated to 2014Q3, and the Irish Energy-Data Nexus is dominated by multinational firm activity.

papers.title: From Individual Learning to Market Equilibrium: Correcting Structural and Parametric Biases in RL Simulations of Economic Models
papers.abstract: Applying Reinforcement Learning (RL) to economic modeling reveals a fundamental tension: standard RL agents do not behave as competitive price-takers. While macroeconomic models typically assume agents take aggregate conditions as given, a naive single-agent RL algorithm learns to internalize its impact on the environment, effectively exerting market power. We illustrate this divergence in a search-and-matching model with concave production, showing that a standard RL agent converges to a monopsonistic allocation rather than the competitive equilibrium. Furthermore, we show that RL's approach to time discounting distorts standard intertemporal economic trade-offs. To resolve these issues, we propose a Calibrated Mean-Field Reinforcement Learning framework that restricts the agent to optimize against an exogenous aggregate state to restore price-taking behavior, and recalibrates the RL reward structure to reflect true economic opportunity costs. By iteratively updating the aggregate state, our algorithm converges to a stationary fixed point that recovers the competitive equilibrium. This approach provides a method for embedding learning algorithms into dynamic general equilibrium models.

papers.title: A Financial Brain Scan of the LLM
papers.abstract: We use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to "brain scan" large language models, mapping internal activations to interpretable concepts and enabling targeted "steering" of specific features. We show that prompting models to adopt specific preferences activates many unintended concepts, complicating causal inference. In contrast, SAEs permit smooth, more isolated steering of target concepts. Furthermore, our scans reveal a stark disconnect between the model's internal feature contributions and its self-generated explanations, showing that these explanations are unreliable guides to its reasoning. Finally, SAEs provide a lightweight intervention for existing models, producing interpretable embeddings and allowing researchers to attenuate specific economic biases.

papers.title: Experimentally Validated Digital Twins: Evaluating Workforce Training Programs in the Age of Big Data
papers.abstract: Modern program evaluation prioritizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) because prior research found that observational estimates of program impacts often diverge substantially from experimental benchmarks. We revisit this finding --- which was based on small survey datasets --- in the era of large-scale administrative data. Using anonymized income tax records covering all American adults between 1999 and 2025, we estimate the effects of workforce training programs on earnings by using machine learning models to predict counterfactuals from rich data on prior work histories, demographics, and residential locations. Rather than testing whether our observational estimates are unbiased, we use 37 RCTs to estimate the distribution of their bias. We find that our machine learning estimates closely match the RCT estimates, with root mean squared error (RMSE) comparable to that of the RCTs themselves. Our method reduces RMSE by 60% relative to parametric estimators used in prior work because our larger samples and richer covariates permit more flexible, higher-dimensional models of the counterfactual. Applying our method to a broader set of sites and enrollment years beyond the experimental sample, we find that treatment effects on earnings vary substantially across locations and over time, even within a given program. Programs that place more participants into target-sector jobs generate the largest earnings gains, with impacts that persist even after participants leave their initial jobs. These findings provide guidance for improving job training programs and, more broadly, illustrate a scalable approach to program evaluation that uses observational data to construct experimentally validated ``digital twins.''

papers.title: Prizes, Shared Hazard, and the Speed of Frontier AI
papers.abstract: Frontier AI labs compete in a contest for commercial leadership while sharing the risk of catastrophe. Each lab gains from arriving earlier but bears only part of the hazard its speed adds, which this paper calls the hazard externality. In an illustrative calibrated takeoff model, three racing labs get through the takeoff period in 18 months, while a common rule on research shares would stretch it to 69 months. Neither force alone explains racing that fast. Removing the contest first closes over ninety percent of the gap in catastrophe probability between racing and a common rule when the catastrophe probability at full speed is 75 percent, and 69 percent when it is 25 percent; averaged over both orders of removal, the contest explains 65 and 44 percent. More labs make each lab race harder, when industry hazard at a common research share does not depend on the number of labs. Under open source in its ideal form, where every lab publishes its capability findings at once, labs slow to the coordinated pace, because no lab can get ahead and each bears all the hazard its research adds. One lab's restraint achieves much less than a common rule. The White House Accord on Super Intelligence of September 2026 audits safety but sets no limit on speed. In the model it does not slow the race, because each lab still gains as much from speeding up.

papers.title: Agreements Have a Clock: Compute Growth and the Verification of AI Restraint
papers.abstract: Rival powers have agreed to limit nuclear arms, phase out ozone-depleting chemicals, and cut greenhouse gases, though each agreement was hard to reach. This paper asks what an agreement to pause frontier AI needs. A follower advances through own research and diffusion from the leader. Because diffusion fades as the gap closes, a paused leader stays ahead longer than its raw lead suggests. A solved agreement game adds voluntary entry, costly monitoring, secret advances, and credible responses. Cooperation is supportable when the monitoring needed to deter a breakout costs no more than either country gains from cooperating. As compute grows during a pause, a secret advance reaches the frozen frontier sooner, shrinking the response window: agreements have a clock. In an example with a fixed leader window, cooperation is supportable through month 18.9. Verified matched safety research extends this to month 25.5, and halving the monitoring cost to month 31.8.

papers.title: Left-Digit Bias: Theory and Empirical Evidence from a Tax Salience Experiment
papers.abstract: Demand often drops sharply at whole-dollar prices. To explain this phenomenon, known as left-digit bias, we develop a random utility model in which consumers consider a good only if its price is below a heterogeneous attention threshold. Masses of consumers with integer attention thresholds generate demand discontinuities. When a tax is introduced, the model predicts a weaker demand response compared to rational choice for left-digit biased consumers. Using data from a tax experiment, we find that the model matches behavioral moments and partially identify the distribution of willingness to pay relative to thresholds. A weak demand response need not imply a low excess burden of taxation and understanding the specific mechanism is important for welfare analysis.

papers.title: Voting Biases in Decentralized Autonomous Organization (DAO) Governance
papers.abstract: Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) replace formal managerial authority with collective decision-making, by handing both proposal rights and token-weighted votes directly to community members. Yet, as in corporate votes, where management sets the agenda and its proposals rarely fail, DAO votes are strikingly one-sided. Using 127 281 proposals and about 51 million votes cast on Snapshot, the leading off-chain DAO voting platform, between 2020 and 2023, we ask which features of the ballot are associated with this support. We relate each choice's voting-power share to three observable features: its position in the list, whether its stance expresses approval, and whether the proposal author selected it. Each identifies one voting bias: position bias, approval bias, and author-selected choice bias. Author-selected choices show the strongest and most robust association, receiving a voting-power share 58.8 percentage points higher than non-author-selected ones, compared with 27.1 percentage points for approving choices and 7.7 percentage points for first-listed ones. About one third of the author bias comes from the author's own voting power; that advantage is smaller in the largest protocols and in proposals with higher participation. The results are robust across alternative specifications and outcomes. Our findings suggest that the agenda power that management holds in corporate voting persists even without a formal hierarchy, and that ballot design and the visibility of proposers' preferences are governance choices rather than neutral implementation details.

papers.title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

papers.title: What Drives Energy Use? Prices, Policy, and Inefficiency
papers.abstract: Why is U.S. energy use so high, even among rich economies? Using a 2006--2022 panel of the 50 states and DC, an LMDI decomposition documents a 12.8% national decline alongside substantial cross-state heterogeneity. To explain differences in energy-use levels across states, we estimate a microfounded stochastic-frontier model and adapt the LMG relative-importance method to the frontier and inefficiency components. Our approach assigns 56.3% of variation to the frontier, 42.2% to inefficiency, and 1.5% to noise. Prices and efficiency-policy environments are the two leading observed contributors, jointly accounting for 31%: prices operate mainly through the benchmark, whereas policy contributes through both components. Their leading ranks are stable across 21 specifications. Persistent low prices, uneven efficiency-policy environments, structural demand, and a sizeable composite inefficiency component help explain high U.S. energy use. Policy should therefore combine durable price signals, coherent efficiency programs, structural investment, targeted measures addressing avoidable energy use, and targeted household support.

papers.title: The Costs and Benefits of Leveraged ETFs
papers.abstract: We study the costs and benefits of leveraged ETFs (LETFs), focusing on five determinants of performance: volatility drag, fees, financing costs, product launches, and market timing. Long broad-equity-index LETFs generated more than 100 billion US dollars in investor gains, including over 40 billion US dollars relative to counterfactual investments in the underlying assets, due to modest structural headwinds and rising markets. Single-stock LETFs, however, are launched on stocks near the top of the volatility and past-return distributions. This caters to retail demand for lottery-like payoffs, but it also creates larger volatility drag, higher financing costs, and greater exposure to losses from poor market timing.
